title: Connection Refused vs. Timeout — The First Branch
intro: The single most useful networking distinction there is: 'connection refused' and 'connection timed out' point at completely different causes. Get this right and you skip half of any debugging session.

steps.prompt: Test port 8080 on 10.0.4.30, giving up after 5 seconds.
steps.fake_output: curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.0.4.30 port 8080: Connection refused
steps.explanation: Refused came back instantly. The host is reachable and actively said 'nothing is listening on that port' (a TCP RST).
steps.why: Refused means the network path WORKS. The problem is on the target host: the service isn't running, crashed, or is listening on a different port or only on localhost. Don't touch firewalls — check the service.

steps.prompt: Now test port 5432 on 10.0.4.31, again with a 5 second limit.
steps.fake_output: nc: connect to 10.0.4.31 port 5432 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
steps.explanation: Timed out: packets went out and nothing at all came back — no acceptance, no refusal.
steps.why: Silence almost always means something in the path is DROPPING packets: a firewall, a cloud security group, a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, or a wrong route. Look at network controls, not the application.

steps.prompt: Scan a small range of ports (20-30) on 10.0.4.31 to see what IS reachable.
steps.fake_output:
Connection to 10.0.4.31 22 port [tcp/ssh] succeeded!
nc: connect to 10.0.4.31 port 25 (tcp) timed out
steps.explanation: SSH on 22 works, so the host is up and routable — only specific ports are being filtered.
steps.why: This confirms it's port-specific filtering (a security group that allows 22 but not 5432) rather than the whole host being down or unreachable.

steps.prompt: On the database host itself, confirm postgres is actually listening and on which address.
steps.explanation: Listening on all interfaces (0.0.0.0). The service is fine — so the timeout is definitely something in the network path dropping traffic.
steps.why: Checking both ends is what turns a guess into a diagnosis: the service is up and listening, yet packets never arrive, which leaves exactly one category of cause — a firewall or security group between them.
